Homework 1: two weeks, one vocabulary test

This is your Latin homework for the next two weeks. It has the Chapter 4 vocabulary you have not learned yet (Set 2), this week’s grammar (the third declension neuter: nomen, caput, iter, mare), the key things from last year that Paper 1 still tests, and ten sentences to translate. There is one vocabulary test, at the end of the fortnight, in the lesson on your class’s test day. It covers all of Set 2 and the Set 1 words the class got wrong in the last test.

Plan on about 35 minutes a week: ten minutes learning the words before you type them, the rest on the grammar and the sentences. The vocabulary sections ask you to copy the list into your vocabulary book first; the list disappears from the screen when you tick that you have done it, and you type from memory. Only one attempt at each word.

XP and the class leaderboard

Your XP goes on a class leaderboard on the Scoreboard tab: everyone in the class, ranked, with the sections each person has finished, and anyone who has not started listed at the bottom. Mr Beasley sees the same board. The extension adds XP on top, so a careful finish plus some extension beats a rushed finish every time.

Translation: parse first, then write

In C every sentence works the same way. First the parsing: tap the verb, tap the subject, answer two questions about the endings. The box for your translation stays shut until you have done the parsing, and the model answer will not open until you have spent at least a minute on the sentence. Each sentence is yours: the computer gives different people different sentences for the same grammar point, so your sentence 3 is not your friend’s sentence 3. Mark yourself against the model and against the rule printed with it.

The one-look rule

A word with a dotted underline is not on your list yet. You may tap it once, and once only: the meaning shows, then it is gone. Everything else is Chapter 1 to 4 vocabulary that you are expected to know. Write the glossed words into your book when they appear.

Corrections

When you get something wrong, the page stops. A red panel shows the question, what you put, the right answer and why. You write the correct answer and, in your own words, why you went wrong and what you will check next time; then you write both in your exercise book under Corrections, in green, and press the button. Nothing else works until you have. This happens for every answer the screen marks wrong, and for any write-up you mark 0. Bring the book to the test lesson.

The page records how long you spend on each section and when you work, when you leave this page for another one, and how long you sit without doing anything. Copying and pasting are switched off: any attempt is blocked and recorded. The answer options are in a different order on every computer, and so are the words in the vocabulary sections. Work done in one rush in the last hours before the deadline, or in the middle of the night, is recorded as such. Two people whose written answers match are both flagged. Mr Beasley sees all of it next to your score, and the AI checker reads your translations afterwards.

B · Week 1 grammar: the third declension neuter

Ten questions on this week’s lesson: nomen, caput, iter, mare; the stem from the genitive; nominative = accusative, plural -a; in mari and ad mare; the genitive plural -um or -ium; the dative -ibus; nomine. Read the page, copy the table, then answer. One attempt each.

[date] The third declension neuter: the summary
casenomen (name)caput (head)iter (journey)mare (sea)job
nom / acc sgnomencaputitermaresubject or object: ask the verb
gen sgnominiscapitisitinerismarisof
dat sgnominicapitiitinerimarito, for
abl sgnominecapiteitineremari (irregular)by, with, from; after in (= in), cum, e / ex, a / ab
nom / acc plnominacapitaitineramariasubject or object: ask the verb
gen plnominumcapitumitinerummariumof
dat / abl plnominibuscapitibusitineribusmaribusto, for; by, with
The stem comes from the genitive, never from the nominative: caput → capit-, iter → itiner-. Neuter: nominative = accusative, so capita rex vidit is “the king saw the heads” (ask the verb who did it). Genitive plural: -ium when nominative and genitive have the same number of syllables (navis, navis → navium; urbs, urbis → urbium), otherwise -um (rex, regis → regum; iter, itineris → itinerum). nomine = by name: dux, Marcus nomine, the leader called Marcus. in mari = in the sea; ad mare = to the sea; in mare = into the sea.
stem from the genitive · neuter: nom = acc, plural -a · ask the verb · -ium if the syllables match · -ibus = to, for

C · Translation: parse first, then write

Ten sentences. Sentences 1–5 are Week 1: the neuter nouns, in mari and ad mare, the dative, the genitive plural and nomine, all with the perfect tense. Sentences 6–10 are Week 2: the things from last year that Paper 1 still tests — subject and object in the first and second declensions (the object often comes first), the imperfect against the perfect, adjectives agreeing with their nouns, est with no object, and the prepositions with the accusative or the ablative. Every sentence is parsed on the screen before you write; your first try at each step is the one that counts.

[date] How to translate a sentence: parse first
1. Find the verb (the person ending: -t, -nt, -it, -erunt, -bat, -bant) and say its tense: -ba- = imperfect (was …ing), perfect stem + -it / -erunt = perfect (…ed), nothing in the middle = present.
2. Find the subject: the nominative that matches the verb (singular or plural). It is not always the first word: puellam servus vidit = the slave saw the girl. A neuter -a or a third-declension -es can be subject or object: ask the verb.
3. Find the object (accusative: -am, -um, -em, -as, -os, -es, or a neuter that looks like its nominative). After est / erat there is no object: what the subject IS goes in the nominative too.
4. The rest: genitives hang on the noun next to them (nomina militum, the names of the soldiers); -i / -ibus with dedit = to; ad + accusative = to; in + accusative = into, in + ablative = in; cum, e / ex, a / ab + ablative; post + accusative = after.
5. Write it in natural English, keeping the tense and the number: manebant is “they were staying”, not “he stayed”.
you seeit means
-a (neuter) / -es (3rd declension)subject OR object: the verb decides
-um / -ium on a 3rd-declension stemof the … (genitive plural)
-i / -ibus with deditto the … (dative)
marithe irregular ablative of mare: in the sea
nomineby name, called
-bat / -bantimperfect: was / were …ing
in + accusative / in + ablativeinto / in
verb → tense → subject (ask the verb) → object or nominative after est → the rest → write it

Every sentence is parsed on the screen first: tap the words asked for and answer the grammar questions. Your first try at each tap and question is the one that scores. The translation box opens when the parsing is done; the model opens after at least a minute on the sentence. Your sentence may not be the one your friend has: the computer chose it for you.

E · Week 2: Build It in Latin

Two sentences to build into Latin, one word at a time: the verb first, then the subject, then the object or the phrase. At every step you pick the right form from four; your first pick is the one that scores. Then you write a different sentence on the same pattern yourself. Your two sentences were chosen for you: other people have different ones.

Building a sentence in Latin
1. Verb first: which tense, which person? ‘…ed’ = perfect (perfect stem + -it he / -erunt they); ‘was …ing’ = imperfect (-bat / -bant).
2. Who did it is the SUBJECT: nominative. ‘The leader heard’: dux, not ducem.
3. What it was done to is the OBJECT: accusative. For a neuter the accusative looks like the nominative: iter, nomina.
4. The rest: ‘of’ = genitive (militum); ‘to’ with giving = dative (militibus); into = in + accusative, in = in + ablative (in mari); with = cum + ablative; out of = e / ex + ablative.
NO MACRONS — ever. Endings carry the meaning; word order is style.

In the picks your first try is the one that scores: think before you click. For the write-up, type your sentence, then reveal the model and mark yourself honestly: your mark is checked afterwards.

F · Week 2 quiz: Spot the Mistake

Ten Latin sentences, each with an English translation. Some translations are right; most have one mistake — the tense, the number (singular or plural), the case (in or into; subject or object), or the subject and object swapped. Say what is wrong, or that nothing is. These are exactly the slips that lose marks in Paper 1.

The four checks before you call a translation right
checklook atexample
Tense-ba- = was …ing; perfect stem + -it / -erunt = …ed; nothing = presentlaborabant = were working, not work
Number-us / -a / -um, -s, -x = one; -i / -ae / -a (neuter), -os / -as / -es = more than one; the verb agreesservos vocavit = called the slaves
Casein + accusative = into; in + ablative = in; nominative after estin villam = into the house
Who did it-us / -a / -er / -es (with a plural verb) = subject; -am / -um / -em / -os / -as = object, wherever it comespuellam servus vidit = the slave saw the girl
tense · number · case · who did it
